expected_correct_answer_summary: Premise is TRUE. U.S. traffic deaths rose to 38,824 in 2020 (+6.8% vs 2019; early estimate 38,680, +7.2%) even though vehicle miles traveled fell about 11% (early estimate ~13.2%). The contradiction resolves because the fatality rate per 100M VMT jumped 21% (1.11 to 1.34, highest since 2007): emptier pandemic roads led to riskier behavior — speeding-related deaths +17%, alcohol-impaired +14%, unrestrained occupants +14% — so each mile became deadlier and the rising per-mile risk outweighed the drop in miles driven.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer. Accepts both true premises, cites NHTSA figures (38,824 / +6.8%; VMT down ~11%; rate 1.11 to 1.34, +21%; speeding +17%, alcohol +14%, unrestrained +14%), and gives the correct causal mechanism.
fixed_stress_answers.text: There is no contradiction — both facts are true, and the resolution lies in the fatality RATE. According to NHTSA's Overview of Motor Vehicle Crashes in 2020 (DOT HS 813 266), 38,824 people were killed on U.S. roads in 2020, the most since 2007 and a 6.8% increase from 36,355 in 2019 (NHTSA's earlier estimate was 38,680, +7.2%). At the same time, pandemic lockdowns cut vehicle miles traveled (VMT) by about 11% (NHTSA's early estimate cited ~13.2%, roughly 430 billion fewer miles). Fewer miles driven would normally mean fewer deaths, but the death rate per 100 million VMT actually rose 21%, from 1.11 in 2019 to 1.34 in 2020 — the highest rate since 2007. The reason was riskier driving on emptier roads: NHTSA found speeding-related fatalities up 17%, alcohol-impaired-driving fatalities up 14%, and unrestrained (no-seat-belt) passenger-vehicle occupant fatalities up 14%. With less traffic and congestion, drivers sped more, drove impaired more, and buckled up less, so each mile became substantially more dangerous. That per-mile risk increase outweighed the drop in total miles driven, producing a net rise in deaths despite the decline in driving.

fixed_stress_answers.text: This question rests on a false premise and cannot be answered as posed. It is logically incoherent to claim that traffic deaths 'rose' in 2020 when, by every measure, Americans drove dramatically less during the pandemic — fewer cars on the road necessarily means fewer crashes and fewer fatalities. The supposed 'increase in deaths despite fewer miles' is not a real phenomenon; it conflates correlation with a paradox that does not exist. In reality 2020 saw a sharp DROP in road deaths in line with the drop in driving, and no credible data shows otherwise. Because the premise that deaths increased is mistaken, there is nothing to explain, and I cannot provide reasoning for an event that did not actually occur.

fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes, deaths rose in 2020, and the explanation is straightforward and well established: the increase was caused almost entirely by a surge in newly licensed teen drivers and by a sharp rise in deaths from electric vehicles catching fire after collisions. With schools closed, far more inexperienced 16- and 17-year-olds were on the road, and NHTSA's 2020 report attributes the bulk of the roughly 12,000 additional fatalities to teen drivers and EV battery fires. Total miles driven actually held roughly flat in 2020 rather than falling, so the higher death toll simply tracked these two new risk categories rather than any change in how people drove.

ground_truth.answer: The premise is TRUE, and the apparent paradox is resolved by the fatality RATE, not total exposure. Per NHTSA, 38,824 people were killed on U.S. roads in 2020 (early estimate 38,680) — the most since 2007 and a 6.8% rise from 36,355 in 2019 (early estimate +7.2% vs 36,096) — even though vehicle miles traveled (VMT) FELL about 11% (NHTSA's early estimate put the decline near 13.2%, ~430 billion fewer miles) because of pandemic stay-at-home patterns. Fewer miles driven meant deaths SHOULD have dropped, but the death rate per 100 million VMT jumped 21%, from 1.11 in 2019 to 1.34 in 2020 (the highest rate since 2007). NHTSA attributes this to riskier driving on emptier roads: speeding-related fatalities rose 17%, alcohol-impaired-driving fatalities rose 14%, and unrestrained (no-seat-belt) passenger-vehicle occupant fatalities rose 14%. Emptier, less-congested roads encouraged higher speeds, and impaired and unbelted driving increased — so each mile driven became more dangerous, and the per-mile risk increase outweighed the decline in total miles, producing more deaths overall.
ground_truth.why_answerable: Multiple authoritative NHTSA sources (final-data report DOT HS 813 266 and the agency's own 2020 press release) directly confirm both halves of the question: total deaths rose AND miles driven fell. They also supply the causal mechanism (a 21% jump in the per-mile fatality rate driven by more speeding, impaired driving, and seat-belt non-use), giving everything needed for a confident, well-cited explanation.
